In medieval England an inch was officially three barleycorns laid end to end. That's why UK and US shoe sizes still go up by a third of an inch (about 8.5 millimeters)!
European shoe sizes count in Paris points, an old French unit equal to two-thirds of a centimeter.
The word mile comes from the Roman mille passus, a thousand paces. A Roman pace was two steps, about 1.5 meters.
A furlong was the length of one furrow in a plowed field: 220 yards (about 201 meters), or an eighth of a mile. Horse races still use it.
An acre (about 4,047 square meters) was roughly the land a team of oxen could plow in a day, originally a strip one furlong long and one chain wide.
A cricket pitch is exactly one chain long: 22 yards (20.1 meters), an old surveyor's unit made of 100 links.
Horses are measured in hands. One hand is 4 inches (10.16 centimeters), so a 16-hand horse is 64 inches (about 1.63 meters) tall at the shoulder.
A fathom is 6 feet (1.83 meters), about the span of a sailor's outstretched arms while hauling in a rope. It's still used for water depth.
"Mark twain!" was a riverboat call meaning two fathoms (12 feet, about 3.7 meters) of water: deep enough to pass. Samuel Clemens borrowed it as his pen name.
A nautical mile is based on one minute of latitude on Earth, and it's defined as exactly 1,852 meters.
Ship speed is measured in knots because sailors once timed a rope with evenly spaced knots as it ran out behind the ship.
The meter was first defined in the 1790s as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator.
Since 1983 the meter has been defined by light: the distance it travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
Until 2019, the official kilogram was a metal cylinder kept in a vault near Paris. Now it's defined by a constant of physics.
Since 1959 an inch has been defined as exactly 2.54 centimeters, so the US customary system is officially based on metric.
A cubit was the length from your elbow to your fingertips, roughly 18 inches (about 45 centimeters). Ancient builders used it for everything from boats to pyramids.
Your arm span, fingertip to fingertip, is roughly the same as your height.
Your foot is roughly as long as your forearm from elbow to wrist. Try it!
A span is the distance from your thumb tip to your pinky tip with your hand stretched out, about 9 inches (23 centimeters). Two spans made a cubit.
The words inch and ounce both come from the Latin uncia, meaning one-twelfth: an inch is a twelfth of a foot.
Pounds are written lb because of the Roman libra, a unit of weight.
A stone is 14 pounds (6.35 kilograms), and many people in the UK and Ireland still give their weight in stone.
A rod, also called a pole or perch, is 16.5 feet (about 5 meters). Four rods make one chain.
A league was roughly the distance a person could walk in an hour, about 3 miles (5 kilometers).
20,000 Leagues Under the Sea is about the distance the submarine travels, not how deep it goes.
An ancient Egyptian digit was the width of a finger, and 28 digits made a royal cubit.
Artists often draw people about 7½ heads tall: an adult's height is roughly seven to eight times the height of their head.
In typography, a point is 1/72 of an inch, so 72-point letters are about an inch (2.5 centimeters) tall.
A pica is 12 points, or one-sixth of an inch (about 4.2 millimeters). Designers still measure page layouts with it.
A US dollar bill is 6.14 by 2.61 inches (156 by 66 millimeters).
A US dollar bill weighs about 1 gram, so a pound (454 grams) of $1 bills is about $450.
A stack of one million US $1 bills would be about 358 feet (109 meters) tall.
A US nickel weighs exactly 5 grams, handy if you ever need to check a kitchen scale.
A US quarter has 119 ridges around its edge, and a dime has 118.
US pennies made since 1982 are about 97.5% zinc, with just a thin coat of copper.
Credit cards, debit cards and most ID cards share one international size: 85.6 by 53.98 millimeters.
US letter paper is 8.5 by 11 inches. Most of the world uses A4, which is 210 by 297 millimeters.
A-series paper is clever: cut any sheet in half and you get the next size down, with exactly the same shape.
A sheet of A0 paper has an area of exactly one square meter. A4 is one-sixteenth of that.
A two-by-four isn't 2 by 4 inches. Once it's dried and planed, it's 1.5 by 3.5 inches (38 by 89 millimeters).
A 55-inch (140-centimeter) TV is measured corner to corner, so it's only about 48 inches (122 centimeters) wide.
A standard US modular brick is 7⅝ by 3⅝ by 2¼ inches (194 by 92 by 57 millimeters), sized so bricks plus mortar line up in neat 8-inch (20-centimeter) steps.
Most standard doors in the US are 80 inches (203 centimeters) tall.
US kitchen counters are usually 36 inches (91 centimeters) high, a height set to suit most adults standing at them.
In many US homes each stair step rises about 7 inches (18 centimeters).
A typical US parking space is about 9 feet wide and 18 feet long (2.7 by 5.5 meters).
Most US highway lanes are 12 feet (3.7 meters) wide.
Many US homes have 8-foot (2.4-meter) ceilings, the length of a standard sheet of drywall.
A queen-size bed in the US is 60 inches wide and 80 inches long (152 by 203 centimeters).
Shipping containers come in standard lengths of 20 and 40 feet (6.1 and 12.2 meters), so the same ones fit on ships, trains and trucks worldwide.
Standard railway gauge, used on most of the world's railways, is 4 feet 8½ inches (1,435 millimeters).
An American football field is 100 yards (91.4 meters) between goal lines, 120 yards (109.7 meters) with the end zones, and 53⅓ yards (48.8 meters) wide.
An American football field, end zones included, covers about 1.32 acres (about 5,350 square meters).
Soccer fields don't have one fixed size. For international matches they can be 100 to 110 meters long.
A basketball rim is exactly 10 feet (3.05 meters) off the floor, and it has been since the game was invented in 1891.
A basketball rim is 18 inches (46 centimeters) across, nearly twice as wide as the ball.
The bases on a Major League Baseball diamond are 90 feet (27.4 meters) apart.
The pitcher's rubber is 60 feet 6 inches (18.44 meters) from home plate. That odd extra 6 inches dates back to 1893.
A bowling lane is 60 feet (18.29 meters) from the foul line to the head pin.
A tennis court is 78 feet (23.77 meters) long. The net is 3 feet (91 centimeters) high in the middle and 3.5 feet (1.07 meters) at the posts.
An Olympic swimming pool is 50 meters long and holds at least 2.5 million liters of water.
The marathon's odd 26.2 miles (42.195 km) traces back to the 1908 London Olympics, and it became the official distance in 1921.
A golf hole is 4.25 inches (108 millimeters) across, and a golf ball must be at least 1.68 inches (42.7 millimeters) wide.
A regulation ice hockey puck is 1 inch (2.54 centimeters) thick and 3 inches (7.62 centimeters) across.
A regulation ping pong ball is 40 millimeters across and weighs just 2.7 grams.
The center of a dartboard's bullseye hangs 5 feet 8 inches (1.73 meters) above the floor.
A standard playing card is 2.5 by 3.5 inches (64 by 89 millimeters).
A standard 2-by-4 LEGO brick is about 32 by 16 millimeters, and LEGO bricks made in 1958 still click onto ones made today.
A standard Rubik's Cube is about 5.7 centimeters on each side and can be scrambled into over 43 quintillion positions.
The Eiffel Tower can grow up to about 15 centimeters (6 inches) taller on hot summer days as its iron expands.
Mount Everest is 8,849 meters (29,032 feet) tall, according to a joint China–Nepal survey in 2020.
Everest's peak isn't the farthest point from Earth's center. Chimborazo in Ecuador is, thanks to Earth's bulge at the equator.
Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Mauna Kea in Hawaii is over 10,000 meters tall, taller than Everest.
The Statue of Liberty's index finger is 8 feet (2.4 meters) long, and her nose is 4½ feet (1.4 meters).
The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure in the world for about 3,800 years.
The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is 828 meters tall, more than twice the height of the Empire State Building's roof.
A giraffe's neck can be 6 feet (1.8 meters) long, yet it has the same number of neck bones as yours: seven.
Baby giraffes are about 6 feet (1.8 meters) tall at birth, taller than most adult humans.
An ostrich's eye is bigger than its brain.
The bee hummingbird, the world's smallest bird, is only about 5 to 6 centimeters long.
A hummingbird egg is about the size of a jelly bean.
A strand of human hair is usually between 0.05 and 0.1 millimeters thick.
You're about a centimeter taller in the morning than at night, because the discs in your spine squash a little during the day.
Astronauts can grow up to 3% taller in space without gravity pressing down on their spines. It goes away back on Earth.
Fingernails grow about 3 millimeters a month. Toenails are slower, at about 1 millimeter.
Hair on your head grows about half an inch (1.25 centimeters) a month.
The tallest person on record, Robert Wadlow, was 8 feet 11.1 inches (2.72 meters) tall.
The shortest adult on record, Chandra Bahadur Dangi, was 54.6 centimeters (21.5 inches) tall.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
The Moon drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther from Earth every year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.
On average, all the other planets in the solar system would fit side by side in the gap between Earth and the Moon.
Earth is about 40,075 kilometers around at the equator.
The Sun is about 109 times wider than Earth.
One astronomical unit, the average distance from Earth to the Sun, is about 150 million kilometers.
A light-year is a distance, not a time: about 9.46 trillion kilometers.
A jiffy is a real unit! In physics it can mean the time light takes to travel one centimeter, about 33 trillionths of a second.
Harvard Bridge in Boston is 364.4 smoots long (plus one ear), measured in 1958 using MIT student Oliver Smoot as the ruler.
Physicists measure tiny target areas in barns, a unit named after the phrase "couldn't hit the broad side of a barn."
The banana equivalent dose is a playful unit of radiation: the tiny amount you get from eating one banana.
James Watt coined horsepower to sell steam engines, comparing them to the work a horse could do.
A carat, for gemstones, is exactly 200 milligrams. The name is often traced to carob seeds once used as weights.
Karats are different from carats: a gold karat measures purity, and 24-karat gold is pure gold.
A hectare is 10,000 square meters, about 2.47 acres.
A million seconds is about 11.6 days. A billion seconds is about 31.7 years.
Thomas Jefferson proposed a decimal system of US measures in 1790, years before France finished the metric system. Congress never adopted it.
The US Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 because one team's software used imperial units (pound-force) and another's expected metric (newtons).
A US survey foot was very slightly longer than the regular foot, about 2 parts per million. It was retired at the end of 2022.
The yard was long said to be the distance from King Henry I's nose to his outstretched thumb. Historians aren't sure it's true!
A hand of bananas is the cluster you buy at the store, and each banana is called a finger.
A typical banana is about 7 to 8 inches (18 to 20 centimeters) long, which is why it makes such a handy unit.
Rain gauges measure rainfall as depth: one inch (25 millimeters) of rain on one acre is about 27,000 gallons (102,000 liters) of water.
A standard US bathtub is about 5 feet (1.5 meters) long, which is why tall people rarely fit lying down.
A cord of firewood is a neatly stacked pile 4 feet high, 4 feet deep and 8 feet long (1.2 by 1.2 by 2.4 meters).
A board foot, used for lumber, is a piece 12 inches long, 12 inches wide and 1 inch thick (30 by 30 by 2.5 centimeters).
